claims.text: Internal thermal stresses are the unifying cause of tensile creep, microhardness evolution, elastic-modulus variation, and aging-induced hardening in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed identically synthesized initial HfNbTaTiZr material can be made single phase before post-solidification treatment.
Post-solidification heat treatment can controllably increase or minimize local lattice-parameter heterogeneity in HfNbTaTiZr.
HfNbTaTiZr can develop local compositional heterogeneity during solidification.
HfNbTaTiZr can contain two BCC phases after cooling because Ta and Zr segregate during solidification.
Local lattice-parameter variations cause thermal-expansion mismatch.
Thermal-expansion mismatch associated with compositional and lattice variations produces internal thermal stresses during high-temperature operation.
The resulting internal stresses modulate dislocation mobility.
The resulting internal stresses influence precipitation during aging.
Precipitate distributions can affect tensile mechanical behavior in alloys derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system.
Internal thermal stresses alter the alloy's elastic response.
Enhanced lattice heterogeneity will increase the tensile creep rate relative to the minimized-heterogeneity baseline.
Enhanced lattice heterogeneity will likely lower yield strength relative to the baseline.
Enhanced heterogeneity will produce a more pronounced work-hardening region.
Enhanced lattice heterogeneity will produce measurable shifts in thermoelastic modulus.
The predicted differences will be strongest near 1250 °C because thermal-expansion effects are maximized there.
Minimizing local lattice-parameter differences suppresses thermal-expansion-mismatch effects.
Segregation is an alternative microstructural factor that may influence measured mechanical responses.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis can be read as saying lattice-parameter inhomogeneity arises from thermal-expansion mismatch, whereas the mediator and mechanism state that lattice-parameter heterogeneity causes the mismatch.

The hypothesis claims to unify cold-rolling microhardness and thermoelastic behavior extending down to 293 K, but the proposed applicability and tests begin at 600 °C and therefore do not directly cover the low-temperature or cold-rolling regimes.
